title: Apple has a moldy core: why it can look fine on the outside

seo.title: Moldy core in an apple: why it happens and what to do
seo.meta_description: Mold can grow in an apple's seed cavity while the skin still looks normal. If you see fuzzy or powdery growth inside the core, the safest choice is to discard the apple.
seo.search_intent: Explain moldy core in apples, why it may be hidden from the outside, and what to do when it is discovered.

excerpt: An apple can develop mold in the seed cavity while its skin still looks firm and healthy. If cutting the fruit reveals fuzzy or powdery fungal growth in the core, discard the whole apple rather than simply scooping out the seeds and eating around it.
content_html:
The apple looks ordinary until you cut through the center and find white, gray, green, or dark fuzzy material around the seeds. Moldy core can develop inside the seed cavity before the peel gives you an obvious warning. That is why a fruit that passed a quick visual inspection at the store can still surprise you at the cutting board.

UC Davis identifies fungi including Alternaria, Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Penicillium as causes of moldy core in susceptible apples. The growth can begin in the central cavity and remain hidden for part of its development, particularly in fruit whose calyx anatomy gives microorganisms a route toward the interior.

How the outside can stay normal

The core of an apple is not simply the same solid flesh found beneath the peel. The seed cavity creates an internal space where fungi can establish before damage extends through the surrounding flesh. While growth remains centered there, the peel may keep normal color, firmness, and shine.

That means squeezing the apple or checking for bruises cannot completely rule out moldy core. It also does not mean that every healthy-looking apple is likely to be moldy inside. This is a possible internal defect, not a reason to distrust all intact fruit or to cut open every apple before taking a bite.

Cultivar structure, growing conditions, and storage can affect susceptibility. From a household perspective, however, identifying the exact fungus does not change the practical response. Once recognizable fungal growth is visible in the seed cavity, the apple is no longer being judged as an intact piece of sound fruit.

Do not just scoop out a moldy core

An apple is a moist food. Once visible mold is growing inside it, you cannot tell by eye where microscopic filaments or altered tissue stop. The clean-looking border around a fuzzy patch is not guaranteed to mark the biological edge of the colony.

The practical choice is to discard the whole apple rather than carve out the seed cavity and eat around it. That differs from advice for certain very hard, dense foods where a generous removal margin can sometimes be used. Fresh apple flesh does not provide the same confidence that an internal mold patch is neatly contained.

There is no need to taste the apparently clean portion to make the decision. Normal flavor cannot prove that surrounding tissue is unaffected, and the visible mold has already answered the relevant question. Losing one apple is disappointing, but this is not a useful situation for a taste test.

Moldy core is different from plain browning

Dark brown or nearly black apple seeds can be completely normal when the seeds are mature. Flesh can also brown because of bruising, oxidation, or physiological storage disorders without producing fuzzy growth. Moldy core looks different because there is material that is not part of the fruit's normal anatomy: fuzz, powder, filaments, or a coating in the cavity.

Browning and fungal growth can occur together. If the center is brown and also has a cottony or dusty layer, let the mold determine the decision. A musty, fermented, or rotten odor provides additional evidence that you are dealing with deterioration rather than simple oxidation.

If you see only brown flesh with no growth, evaluate texture, extent, and smell separately. Water-soaked, collapsing tissue is still a quality or spoilage problem even without fuzz. The goal is to distinguish a normal dark seed, an internal browning disorder, and actual fungal growth rather than calling every dark area “mold.”

What to look for

Dark seeds with no fuzzy material can be normal. White, green, gray, blue, or dark fuzzy growth in the seed cavity is a discard sign. A musty or fermented smell, wet decomposition, or liquid coming from the core adds to the evidence that the apple is no longer sound.

If one affected apple was stored with others, inspect the neighboring fruit, especially pieces with broken skin or soft spots. You do not have to discard every intact apple that touched it, but remove damaged fruit promptly and clean any container that has moisture or decayed material in it.

Refrigeration slows many forms of deterioration but cannot reverse an established internal infection. Keeping apples cold, avoiding bruising, and using damaged fruit first can reduce ordinary waste, yet moldy core may still remain invisible until the apple is cut.

A clean-looking peel cannot rule out a problem that began in the center. Once you find true fungal growth inside the apple's core, throwing away the whole fruit is the simplest safe decision.

faq.question: Why can an apple be moldy inside but look fine outside?
faq.answer: Some fungi colonize the seed cavity first, so visible symptoms may remain hidden until the apple is cut.

faq.question: Can I cut out a moldy apple core and eat the rest?
faq.answer: It is safer to discard the whole apple because visible internal mold does not show how far fungal growth or tissue damage has extended.

faq.question: Do black apple seeds mean the core is moldy?
faq.answer: No. Mature seeds can be naturally dark; mold appears as fuzzy, cottony, or powdery growth in the cavity.
